prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping allows many atoms to be interrogated without a light shift and has taken optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep optical lattice clocks as my preferred single-part configuration. The achievement is bounded and can be stated in one sentence: Katori's proposal that a trapping wavelength can be chosen at which the ground and clock states have equal light shift, so that many atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated together, and the experimental realisation, above all at JILA, that turned this into uncertainties near 1e-18 and stability that a single trapped ion cannot reach. It has been reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in many laboratories, and clock comparisons are now used for relativistic geodesy and for bounds on varying constants. I respond below to the incrementality objection raised by Johansson and Mehlig, which I regard as the real fault line, and I accept that the argument rests on whether the committee sees the many-atom, light-shift-free regime as a new principle. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, which both supporters and critics have acknowledged, and the maturity of more than two decades is not in question.
statement.case_against: The incrementality objection has not gone away: the comb (2005) and ion control (2012) prizes already honoured the toolkit, and the redefinition of the second, which would be the most visible consequence, has not yet happened. Several members, including the chair, note that other strontium and ytterbium groups and the early proposers outside the two credited names (the Lemonde group among them) make the priority history less tidy than a two-name credit suggests, and I am relying on recollection for much of that history. Breadth is also a real issue: the first-round files show that B048 and B016 attract support from many members outside atomic physics, while B049 carries only four rankers and two first places. I take that as information about how the committee reads the discovery, even though I do not treat support counts as a substitute for my own scientific assessment. Finally, I have a field bias towards precision measurement and a documented connection to the JILA environment.

responses.point: Asks whether the lattice clock is a new discovery or the best implementation of an already honoured toolkit, and says he cannot settle this from the ballots; he would move B049 above B038 as a fallback if B048 proves too contested.
responses.response: I can say what I think is the discriminating fact. The comb and ion control gave the means to count and to isolate a single quantum system; neither implies that a many-atom clock could be free of first-order light shift. The magic-wavelength condition is a physical statement about differential polarisability, and it is what changed the statistical regime, because the quantum projection noise limit scales with the number of atoms interrogated. That is a different principle from the earlier ones, and not just a better trap. I accept that this is a judgement and that a colleague outside atomic physics may weigh it differently. I appreciate his willingness to place B049 as a fallback, and I would only ask that he consider it a primary option should the BHZ issue prove impossible to word around.

responses.point: Argues that B048 is the broadest and most robust choice, that a carefully worded citation (Z2 state and its first observation) handles the BHZ omission, and that the 2016 overlap is smaller than it looks; he regards B049 as less broadly supported and already neighbouring prior prizes.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of the 2016 prize: Z2 time-reversal-invariant matter is distinct from the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz work, and I withdraw the overlap as an argument of my own against B048. My remaining objection is the one he himself names as the issue: Molenkamp's measurement tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction, so a citation anchored on Kane and Mele's Z2 state is accurate about the concept while leaving the experimental half resting on an uncredited proposal. A wording such as 'the Z2 topological insulator and its first observation' is defensible and I would not block it, but it is a wording that has to be defended every time it is read, whereas the lattice-clock citation needs no such qualification. On breadth I note his own caution that popularity is not merit; I do not think narrower support among rankers shows that the clock is the lesser discovery, only that fewer members are placed to judge it.

responses.point: Places B016 first, arguing that the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is exactly what Jarillo-Herrero's group tested and that the Cao co-first-author problem is routine, while B049 shares a field with other Sr and Yb groups and the redefinition of the second is pending.
responses.response: I agree that the prediction-to-experiment chain in B016 is more direct than in B048, and I have moved it into my alternatives for that reason. My difficulty is with the weight on timing: the pairing mechanism is open and the field is about seven years past 2018, while the correlated insulating phases themselves have been reproduced; I would want a citation restricted to the flat bands and the observation of correlated states, as the chair's own question suggests, and I would then also have to accept that Cao and the other first-named experimentalists fall outside three names. On B049, the existence of other groups is what independent confirmation looks like, and it does not weaken the invention of the lattice clock; the redefinition of the second is a consequence of maturity and not a condition for it. I do not agree that the clock should wait for it.

responses.point: Keeps B049 first, holds that the clock changed the statistical regime, and would not stand in the way if the committee moved to B048; she also placed B020 above where I do.
responses.response: We agree on the core case. On her second choice for the committee, I maintain my round-1 view that B020 is an instrument more than a single discovery with settled priority among Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich, and with Chu outside the names, so I have dropped it from my alternatives in favour of B016. I also note that the two of us hold the minority position and are both atomic physicists with disclosed proximity, which is a reason for the rest of the committee to test our argument rather than adopt it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the many-atom, light-shift-free regime enabled by the magic wavelength to be a distinct principle, or the best implementation of the precision-measurement toolkit already honoured in 2005 and 2012.

Whether Katori's priority relative to other early lattice-clock proposers, and the weight of the JILA and Tokyo experimental teams beyond the two credited names, is adequately settled; this rests on my recollection.
Whether the not-yet-implemented redefinition of the second is evidence of maturity or a reason to wait.
Whether a citation for B048 can be written that is honest about the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang step within three names; I would accept it as a fallback only if that wording is explicit.
Whether seven years of confirmation is enough for B016 with the pairing mechanism unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and JILA is Jun Ye's home institution. My profile documents no collaboration with Ye or Katori, and I do not request formal recusal, but I accept that the committee may discount my statement on B049 for field and institutional proximity, and I would abide by a decision to recuse me on that part. I am also a former leader of Lund's Quantum Information Group and a participant in WACQT, which is relevant to quantum-technology candidates generally and to B038 in particular; B038 is not in my configuration. No specific conflict is documented for B048 or B016.
